title: How Long Do Breast Implants Last? When to Replace Them
meta_description: No fixed date: the FDA says implant life varies and can't be predicted. They aren't lifetime devices, but 10 years alone is no reason to replace them.
excerpt: There is no expiry date on a breast implant, and the every-10-years rule is a myth. Here is what the FDA actually says, what the makers' 10-year studies show, when replacement really comes up, and how to keep track of your implants over the years.
quick_answer:
How long do breast implants last?

No one can give a number. The FDA says implants are not lifetime devices and that their life varies by person and cannot be predicted. It sets no replacement date, so 10 years alone is not a reason to replace them. In the makers' studies, 24% to 36.5% of women had another operation within 10 years of a first augmentation.

sources.title: Things to Consider Before Getting Breast Implants
quotes: Breast implants are not lifetime devices. The longer you have your implants, the more likely it will be for you to have them removed or replaced.

sources.title: Risks and Complications of Breast Implants
quotes: Normal aging of the implant
Capsular contracture is the hardening of the breast around the implant. It can occur in the tissue surrounding one or both implants. This hardening causes the tissue to tighten, which can be painful.
Grades III and IV capsular contracture are considered severe and may require reoperation.
After removal, some women do not choose to replace their implants. These women may have cosmetically undesirable dimpling, chest wall concavity, puckering, or sagging of their natural breasts.
Women with large breast implants, especially those inserted on top of the chest muscles (subglandularly), may have major cosmetic deformity if they choose not to replace them
most silicone implant ruptures are without symptoms, known as "silent ruptures."

Occasionally when a silicone gel-filled implant ruptures, you may notice a decrease in breast size, change in breast implant shape, hard lumps over the implant or chest area, an uneven appearance of the breasts, pain or tenderness, tingling, swelling, numbness, burning, or changes in sensation.
You and/or your doctor will be able to tell if your saline-filled implant ruptures because the saline solution leaks into your body immediately or over several days and deflates the implant.
There is no guarantee that you will have a satisfactory cosmetic outcome from any reoperation.
